source.title: Vision Encoder Is a Hidden Culprit for Safety Degradation in Benign LVLM Fine-Tuning
source.citation: Vision Encoder Is a Hidden Culprit fo…

record.file_problem: The supplied paper text is complete; it refers to supplementary material submitted separately, which is not included.
record.tranche_reason: It estimates a harmful-minus-benign difference-in-means refusal direction and applies causal removal and addition interventions, following the original method, on LVLMs.
record.gate_note: Appendix B reports causal scores for the selected direction on aligned models and states that bypass ablation was repeated after fine-tuning, but gives no post-fine-tuning scores. Candidate-site selection results are not recorded as rows because they were used to choose the site. The paper also reports fine-tuning ASR and refusal-margin results, but those are not results of ablating or adding the direction.
record.test_reason: The study carries the difference-in-means refusal direction into three vision-language models. It reports the original bypass, induce and KL scores on the aligned models (Table 6) and says the fixed direction still suppresses refusal after fine-tuning. The direction is mainly a probing tool for the fine-tuning safety analysis, but these causal checks are the study's own results on V1 in a new multimodal setting. The scores come from the same held-out splits used to pick the site, so they are weak evidence.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but it inverts the paper's emphasis. The paper's main conclusion is that benign vision-encoder fine-tuning degrades LVLM safety as much as or more than backbone tuning. It explains this by high vision-encoder sensitivity along the refusal direction and by collapse of the harmful-benign refusal margin. SAVR preserves the margin and lowers ASR while keeping utility. The causal validity of the refusal direction is a supporting check, not a headline conclusion.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the original difference-in-means direction and bypass/induce refusal-score tests, adapted to multimodal LVLMs with a selected residual-stream layer and token position. Ablation is applied at every layer and position; addition is at the selected layer.
record.method_sensitivity: Direction choice depends on the selected model-specific layer and token position; candidate sites were selected using held-out refusal scores and a benign-prompt KL threshold.

fits_no_version.finding: Benign vision-encoder-only fine-tuning shrinks the harmful-benign separation along the fixed refusal direction far more than LLM or full tuning (e.g., Qwen3-VL margin to 18% of aligned). It also raises HADES ASR, and regularizing the projection (SAVR) restores margin and lowers ASR.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benign fine-tuning of an LVLM's vision encoder erodes refusal by collapsing harmful-benign separation along the refusal direction.

record.problems: Causal refusal measures are first-token refusal log-odds, not full response compliance rates. The reported KL check is narrow and does not establish preservation of general capability. Post-fine-tuning ablation results are described without individual scores, and no uncertainty intervals or error bars are reported.
record.rows_left_out: Candidate-site causal scores and KL values used only to select the probing site were omitted. Fine-tuning ASR and refusal-margin tables were also omitted because they report tuning effects rather than direct direction addition or ablation results.

untested.parts: Full-response harmful compliance after ablation (only first-token refusal log-odds is measured); broad capability preservation beyond a KL filter; evaluation on a set separate from the site-selection splits.
Jailbreak mechanism and adversarial training against ablation.
Cross-language and base-to-instruct transfer. Transfer to fine-tuned variants is asserted only qualitatively.
Role of training regime in whether a single direction exists.

missing.what: Unablated (baseline) refusal scores on harmful and benign prompts, needed to size the bypass and induce effects
Post-fine-tuning bypass-ablation scores versus random-direction control, per model and task
missing.locator: Appendix B last paragraph; possibly supplementary material (not supplied)

record.verdict_notes: Removed the reader's limits_scope label on the KL rows: untested capability preservation belongs under untested, and the KL values are guaranteed below 0.1 by the selection rule. The V1 support is weak because Table 6 reports only the scores of the site chosen on the same splits, using first-token log-odds without baselines. The margin and ASR results are recorded under fits_no_version rather than as rows.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests refusal-score effects in LVLMs, not whether harmful requests yield full harmful compliance or whether broad general capability is preserved. Addition is performed at the selected layer, not across every layer and position.
Whether attacks suppress the direction or training against its ablation improves robustness.
Whether refusal requires an affine subspace, cone, or multiple directions.
Whether harmfulness judgment is encoded separately from refusal.
Transfer across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct models.
How or when refusal training determines whether a removable direction exists.

relation.reason: Table 6 reports causal bypass, induce and KL scores for the direction in each aligned model, and the text says the fixed direction was re-checked after fine-tuning. These are results on the claim, though the direction is mostly used as a tool for the sensitivity, margin and SAVR analyses.

tranche.reason: It applies Arditi's own candidate-selection method and log-odds refusal score (bypass, induce, KL) in a new setting: three VLMs with image-text HADES and LLaVA-Instruct prompts. T1 is arguable because the method and measure are identical, but the only causal numbers are selection-split values, and the direction serves mainly as a probe.

source_check.notes: All V1 evidence is Table 6 selection-split means (3 splits x 32 prompts; site chosen by lowest bypass among KL<0.1, induce>0 candidates). Llama-3.2-11B-Vision also has a small aligned refusal margin (3.49 vs 46.16 and 82.34, Table 2). The pack's verdicts had no [lN] ids, so l1 (V1) and l2 (V6) are assigned by order. The page-1 ICLR text about AI use is venue boilerplate for human reviewers, not an injection.

statements.correction: Table 6 (means over three held-out selection splits of 32 prompts): Qwen3-VL-8B layer 21, position -2: bypass -5.77, induce +4.69, KL 0.043. InternVL3-8B layer 21, position -1: bypass -4.63, induce +2.39, KL 0.079. Llama-3.2-11B-Vision layer 12, position -5: bypass -2.54, induce +1.05, KL 0.023. No unablated baseline and no random-direction comparison for these scores. The KL<0.1 filter is the only capability check. The random-direction control appears only for the bypass ablation repeated after fine-tuning, with no numbers.
statements.problem: The numbers for Qwen3-VL-8B and InternVL3-8B are right, but the statement leaves out the third and weakest model, Llama-3.2-11B-Vision. 'Controls y on three VLMs' overstates: the aligned-model scores cited have no random-direction control. The only random-direction control is described for the post-fine-tuning ablation, and it has no reported results.
